analysis.one_liner: Shields gun makers and dealers from most lawsuits over crimes committed with their products.
analysis.headline: The House never took a floor vote on H.R. 800, but its Senate twin became federal law that October, giving the firearms industry broad immunity from suits over gun crimes.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill barred virtually all lawsuits in any state or federal court against firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, importers, and their trade associations for harm caused by the criminal or unlawful misuse of their products, and it ordered the immediate dismissal of suits already pending. It kept narrow exceptions, including for negligent sales to obviously dangerous buyers, knowing violations of sale and marketing laws, and defective products. H.R. 800 itself was reported out of committee but never received a House floor vote; an identical Senate bill was enacted instead, so the policy became law anyway.
analysis.who_benefits: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, importers, and their trade associations gain near-total protection from civil liability for harms caused when their products are criminally misused. Shooting victims and their families lose a major avenue for compensation, and cities and states lose the lawsuit tool they had been using to press the industry on distribution practices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits "qualified civil liability actions" in any state or federal court against firearms or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, and trade associations for damages or other relief resulting from criminal or unlawful misuse of their products [S2][S3][S4].
Requires the immediate dismissal of any such lawsuit pending at the time of enactment [S2][S4].

Preserves narrow exceptions, including suits for negligent entrustment, knowing violations of statutes governing sale or marketing, breach of contract or warranty, and product defects when the product is used as intended [S2][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Shooting victims and their families, who lose the ability to sue manufacturers and dealers for harm caused by criminally misused guns; municipalities whose pending suits seeking to recover the costs of gun violence would be dismissed under the bill.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminated pending lawsuits brought by states, municipalities, and private parties against the gun industry — the very actions its findings describe as brought by "the Federal Government, States, municipalities, and private interest groups" — dismissing them immediately rather than letting courts decide them [S4].

The product-defect exception is sharply limited: if a gun's discharge was caused by a volitional criminal act, that act is treated as the sole proximate cause of any resulting harm, so a defect claim is unlikely to succeed in shooting cases [S4].
The bill overrides the tort law of all fifty states, replacing state courts' own liability rules with a single federal shield for one industry.

Supporters' good-faith case: a business that lawfully sells a functioning, heavily regulated product should not be bankrupted by suits over crimes committed by third parties, which is the position codified in the bill's findings [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The industry's argument — that sellers of lawful, federally regulated products should not pay for strangers' crimes — has force as a matter of fairness to individual dealers. But the bill goes far beyond that: it wipes out pending suits by cities and victims, strips the courts of ordinary tort tools for one industry, and leaves victims of gun crimes with almost no civil recourse against the trade that supplied the weapon. The narrow exceptions are hard for most plaintiffs to clear in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill 22-12 and it sat on the Union Calendar without a floor vote, but an identical Senate bill was passed and signed, so the same law took effect anyway.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported by a vote of 22-12 on May 25, 2005, and it was reported with an amendment on June 14, 2005 [S6].
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 70) on June 14, 2005, but the action history shows it never received a House floor vote [S6].
The measure had 257 cosponsors, including 47 Democrats and 210 Republicans [S5].
The sponsor made remarks on the measure on October 26, 2005, the same day the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act was signed into law [S6].
The identical law was enacted through its Senate companion (S. 397), which passed both chambers and was signed by President George W. Bush on October 26, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The firearms industry is far better off: it obtained the statutory immunity through the Senate vehicle even though the House never voted on this bill. Shooting victims and the cities that had pending lawsuits against the industry are worse off, as those suits were dismissed under the new law.

sides.party_line_note: Support was broad but lopsided: 210 of 232 House Republicans cosponsored versus 47 of 202 Democrats, and the committee reported the bill 22-12 on party-leaning lines.

industries.note: The bill grants the industry a federal shield from most civil liability for harm caused when its products are criminally misused, including suits by shooting victims and cities. The industry's gain is victims' loss of recourse in court.

Sellers are covered by the same immunity, protecting them from suits over irresponsible distribution practices except in narrow negligence and knowing-violation cases. Victims lose their claim against the retailers that supplied the guns used against them.

Trade associations are also named as protected defendants, so suits targeting industry-wide conduct through their trade group are barred. This removes a legal avenue cities had used to reach industry-wide practices.
Cities with pending industry suits would have them dismissed immediately. Their interest in the bill ran directly against the industry's.
